sec.title: Objectives:
sec.p: To investigate whether the Cayo Santiago, Puerto Rico (Latitude: 18.1564° N; temperature range 19°C to 32°C) rhesus macaque population has acclimated to their tropical island conditions since arriving from Lucknow, India (Latitude: 26.8470°N; temperature range 8°C to 41°C) in 1938.

sec.title: Materials and Methods:
sec.p: Using the derived skeletal collection, measurements were taken of long bone lengths, diaphyseal circumference, and body weight using 635 (237 males and 398 females) skeletally mature individuals. Measurements sampled colony members born over a 51-year time span at Cayo Santiago, from 1951–2002.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Results demonstrated that body weights and diaphyseal circumferences significantly declined in both males and females. Long bone lengths relative to body weight and diaphyseal circumference also increased in females. Whereas body weight, long bone length and diaphyseal circumference declined at near parallel rates in males.

sec.title: Discussion:
sec.p: The population has acclimated to homogenous, tropical, conditions of the Caribbean island since their arrival over 80 years ago. Trends in both sexes aligned with Bergmann’s rule, though females displayed a greater decline in body weight, as well as greater affinity with Allen’s rule, than did males. Buffering effects related to male competition may be responsible for this discrepancy. Overall, the Cayo Santiago population, as shown over a significant period (1951 to 2002) of their history, have acclimated to their island conditions by decreasing in size and altering body proportions.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Organismal fitness is determined by an ability to survive and reproduce in their current environment (Allen Orr, 2009). When exposed to new environments, organisms tend to respond in order to best maximize fitness under these new pressures. Such responses can be broadly divided into two categories: acclimation and adaptation. The former refers to phenotypic changes that are reversible if the new environmental pressures are removed (Wilson and Franklin, 2002). Occurring on short evolutionary timescales, acclimation ranges in effect from a few minutes to generations. Adaptation, in contrast, refers to changes that have been incorporated into the genotype, often resulting from long-term exposure to particular environmental conditions (Collier et al, 2019).

Climate is the most fundamental determinant of any environment, and thus is largely responsible for not only orchestrating organismal distribution but also its phenotype (Kumar and Kumar, 2018). According to ecogeographic principles, body size and appendage length should vary upon a climatic and latitudinal gradient (Bergmann, 1847; Allen, 1877). Bergmann’s and Allen’s rules predict that populations of a species residing in colder climates will exhibit larger body sizes and shorter extremities than their counterparts in warmer climates (Ruff, 1994; Weinstein, 2011; Huffman et al, 2020). This is based on a surface area/volume ratio that regulates heat expenditure in response to surrounding temperatures (Paterson, 1996). Such patterns have since been intensely studied and debated (Geist, 1987; Meiri and Dayan, 2003; Symonds and Tattersall, 2010) across a wide range of taxa that includes birds (Yom-Tov et al, 2006; Fan et al, 2019) and a variety of mammals (Yom-Tov and Nix, 2008; Alhajeri and Steppan, 2016; Gohli and Voje, 2016). Modern human body proportions have been found to align with Bergmann’s and Allen’s rules, with populations in colder climates associated with wider bi-iliac breadths, larger cranial and ribcage sizes, smaller statures, and greater body masses relative to those closer to the equator (Ruff, 1994; Foster and Collard, 2013; García-Martínez et al, 2018). Conversely, Neanderthal remains effectively highlight many characteristics that are believed to be cold-adapted in the postcrania, including relatively short limbs and distal limb segments (crural/brachial indexes), as well as large diaphyses and articular surfaces (Holliday, 1997; Pearson, 2000; Buck et al, 2018).

There have been similar discoveries in non-human primates. Weinstein (2011) found that macaque species inhabiting colder climatic regions exhibited greater overall body size, smaller limb lengths relative to body size, and greater articular dimensions of the limb bones than those in opposing climates. However, limb proportions were deemed to reflect variation of locomotion preference between species (Kikuchi and Hamada, 2009; Weinstein, 2011). Both inter- and intramembral indices have been found to relate to locomotor mode (Jungers, 1985; Strasser, 1992; Weinstein, 2011; Anapol et al, 2005; Kikuchi and Hamada, 2009), as well as allometric scaling of body size (Jungers, 1985; Demes and Gunther, 1989; Strasser, 1992) and thermoregulatory acclimation, (Trinkhaus, 1981; Holliday, 1997; 1999; Buck et al, 2018; Turner et al, 2018; Serrat et al, 2008). Intraspecific investigations of limb length and proportions (Buck et al, 2018; Turner et al, 2018), cranial size (Fooden and Albrecht, 1993) and relative tail length (Fooden, 1997; Turner et al, 1997; Fooden and Albrecht, 1999; Huffman et al, 2020) have also all yielded support for Bergmann’s and Allen’s rules.

The common practice of translocation, often from the wild into captive settings, has provided an opportunity to investigate the process of acclimation in macaque populations. Paterson (1996) found that the body weights of two wild Macaca fuscata populations acclimatized to the surroundings of their translocated captive settings, with those transplanted to the relatively warm climates of Texas (29.4401°N; 98.6391°W) decreasing in body weight over time and those to the cooler temperatures of Oregon (45.5243°N; 122.8755°W), gaining weight. This not only supported Bergmann’s rule but demonstrated an ability in macaques to acclimate somatically over one or two generations. The author also compared numerous anthropometric measurements between present day members of the two captive locations, finding that the Texas colony exhibited increased body size surface areas, smaller segment circumferences and greater long bone lengths than those of the Oregon colony (Paterson, 1996). A similar study (Clarke and O’Neil, 1999) compared body weight and several anthropometric measurements between (north) China-born Macaca mulatta and their translocated, Louisiana-born (30.4733°N; 90.1246°W) captive offspring. Measurements revealed the Louisiana-born offspring were lighter, had a taller stature, and longer limb bones than their China-born parents, congruent with ecogeographic expectations. The findings are particularly striking, given the morphological response over a single generation in an environmentally and genetically controlled parent-offspring comparison.

Outside the temperature-latitude axiom, several other factors have been found to influence thermoregulatory patterns. For example, greater body sizes have been associated with the ability to buffer against nutritional stress in increasingly seasonal (greater annual temperature range) environments (Boyce, 1978; Murphy, 1985; Macho et al, 1996; Cardini et al, 2007). Slower and prolonged growth rates have alternatively also been suggested to produce larger body sizes in seasonal environments (Vrba, 1996; Cardini et al, 2007; Meiri, 2010). On the other hand, Turner et al (2018) found seasonality (standard deviation of annual mean temperature) to be only weakly associated with body size among Chlorocebus species. The researchers hypothesized the large body size of South African vervets was necessary to stabilize core body temperatures to withstand the coldest extremities of their habitat (Aschoff, 1981; Lubbe et al, 2014; Henzi et al, 2017; Turner et al, 2018). The same mechanism has been postulated in turtles (Sato, 2014) and sharks (Nakamura et al, 2020). Likewise, similar studies in Canids (Martinez et al, 2013), cattle (Collier et al, 2019) and birds (Fan et al, 2019) all emphasize the coldest extremes of an organism’s range to be an important distributor of morphological variation. Several other studies have found that primate body size actually decreases with greater seasonality, yet only in combination with increased rainfall (Turner et al, 1997; Fernandez-Duque, 2011; Plavcan, 2012). Such studies highlight the challenges of tying individual climatic variables to their direct effects on body size, given they are so inextricably linked. Indeed, rainfall itself has frequently been found to correlate with body size due to its direct effect on resource productivity (Cardini et al, 2007; Dunham et al, 2013; Grunstra et al, 2018). The inverse of this problem is the multivariate nature of body size. As well as climate, numerous biosocial factors such as, sexual dimorphism, dominance rank, reproductive seasonality, population density, sex ratio, and competition levels are posited to impact body size (Clutton-Brock and Harvey, 1977; Plavcan, 2002; Plavcan, 2012; Wright et al, 2019; Heldstab et al, 2021). Therefore, due to the interrelated nature of environmental variables and the competing pressures on body size, studies seeking to investigate ecogeographic principles can be difficult to test directly if not appropriately contextualized.

In this study we investigate the acclimation of another translocated population: the Rhesus macaques at Cayo Santiago. Arriving from Lucknow, India in 1938, the population was originally established for biomedical and behavioral research (Carpenter, 1971; Dunbar, 2012). The island measures 15.2 acres, with each individual provisioned with 0.23kg of monkey chow a day (Widdig et al, 2016). Since their arrival, no other free-ranging primate colony has been as comprehensively studied or as closely managed as the Cayo Santiago macaques (Rawlins and Kessler, 1986a; Dunbar, 2012; Wang, 2012; Kessler and Rawlins, 2016; Wang et al, 2016). One of these research projects posed the question of acclimation to the tropical Puerto Rican island. Weinstein (2001) found longer limbs and limb segments in the Cayo Santiago monkeys compared to a sample of wild-shot Asian Rhesus macaques, with no differences found in limb proportions. The author concluded that this extension of absolute limb size, without accompanying differences in crural or brachial indexes, was indicative of a lack of acclimation to the island conditions and instead reflective of the provisioned diet of the Cayo Santiago population. It is plausible that additional measurements leveraging a greater number of the Cayo Santiago skeletons over a majority proportion of their time inhabiting the island elucidates processes not observed in Weinstein’s (2001) seminal research study. Indeed, the research-utility of the population derives partly from Dr Stuart Altmann’s long term observational studies that began in 1956 (Altmann, 1962), where each individuals identity, sex, age, family lineage, and social group affiliation was tracked and continues to be (Dunbar, 2012; Wang et al, 2016). Partly, also, from the systematic collection of skeletal remains that began in 1972 by Donald Sade (Sade, 1972). Therefore, in light of this combination, the colony is not only richly understood, but is uniquely primed for long term studies of secular trends.

Only several studies have investigated secular trends in the morphology in the Cayo Santiago macaques, yet they produce conflicting results. Blomquist and Turnquist (2011) found female cranial and postcranial sizes declined over a 25-year period from 1957 to 1982, despite positive selection for larger sizes. DeRosseau and Reichs (1987) instead found long bone lengths in both sexes generally increased over a 28-year period, from 1951 to 1979. The conflicting patterns in the above studies suggest that thermoregulation may not a principal factor in regulating body size and proportions, which may instead reflect fluctuations in population density and management strategies (DeRosseau and Reichs, 1987; Weinstein, 2001; Blomquist and Turnquist, 2011). Indeed, Lucknow’s (26.8470° N; 80.9349° E) average annual temperature is 29°C while Cayo Santiago’s (18.1564° N; 65.7335° W) is similar at 27°C. However, differences exist within that. Lucknow’s minimum and maximum monthly mean temperatures range between 8°C and 41°C throughout the year, while Cayo Santiago’s range is relatively homogeneous, being limited to 19°C and 32°C. The tropical island receives more hours of annual sunshine (2964 hours) in a smaller number of daylight hours (4356 hours) and at a higher relative humidity (79%) than their origin location (69%) (Wang et al, 2016), as well as significantly higher annual rainfall (2027mm) than Lucknow (814 mm). Over the years, the receding shift of the rainfall season at Cayo Santiago, from late winter to late autumn, has correlated with the onset of the birth season, suggesting the population is responsive to abiotic pressures (Koford, 1965; Vandenbergh and Drickamer, 1973; Rawlins and Kessler, 1985; Hoffman et al, 2008; Kaumanns et al, 2013) (though see Hernández-Pacheco et al, 2016). Therefore, taken together, it is possible the conflicting results of the above studies more likely reflects relatively weak sample size power (Blomquist and Turnquist, 2011; n = 66) (DeRosseau and Reichs, 1987; n = 101) over considerable timespans. This study aims to reconcile sample size inadequacies in previous studies and test for acclimation in the Cayo Santiago macaques. We hypothesize that the homogenous (19°C to 32°C) climate of Cayo Santiago will produce morphological responses akin those acclimating to a more tropical climate. This would predict smaller body weights, increased long bone lengths, smaller long bone diaphyses and relative lengthening of distal limb elements over time.

sec.title: MATERIALS AND METHODS
sec.p: In this study, body weight, limb segment lengths, diaphyses and limb ratios were measured for 635 skeletally mature specimens (398 females, 237 males) across a 51-year timespan (1951 to 2002).

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: All skeletal measurements were taken at the Caribbean Primate Research Center’s (CPRC) Primate Morphology Laboratory at the University of Puerto Rico. This consisted of 635 (398 females, 237 males) skeletally mature individuals (Table 1). The date of birth is known for 635 individuals. Skeletal maturity was based on fully fused (as opposed to fusing) epiphyses in all the long bones employed in this study: two in each of the humerus, radius and tibia, and three in the femur. All linear and diaphyseal measurements of these four long bones are defined in Table 2 and Fig. 1 and were measured by GF (Appendix Tables 1–2). Limb ratios, derived from linear measurements, are defined in Table 2, as well as other cranial and postcranial measurements used in further analysis. Body weight data was collected for 104 individuals (Table 3) and sourced from previous, published (Altmann, 1962) and unpublished investigations, as well as the CPRC databases. Body weight data were provided by Dr. Donald Sade, Dr. Christy Hoffman, Dr. Emma Nelson, Dr. Tara Mandalaywala, Dr. Dario Maestripieri, Dr. Michael Platt, Dr. Karli Watson, and Dr. Michael Heistermann.

sec.title: Quality Control
sec.p: Linear dimensions were measured using digital callipers to the nearest 0.01 millimeter. Diaphyseal dimensions were measured using a Hansmaya tape measure to the nearest millimeter. Measurement error was assessed by calculating the percent ratio between the variance of the method error (squared Dahlberg’s error) and the population variance of that measurement (squared standard deviation) (Wang and Dechow, 2006). Measurements were repeated twice over successive weeks on 12 individuals: 6 males and 6 females, which consisted of two 5-year, 10-year and 15-year-old animals for each sex. For lengths, measurement error accounted for just under 1% of the population variance, apart from the radius (6.15%). For diaphyses, all measurement errors accounted for less than 2% of the population variance. In order to meaningfully match measured skeletal dimensions with known body weights, non-adult (<7 years old) weights were used if they were recorded within a year of recorded death. For adults with single or multiple data recordings, the maximum weight over a lifetime was used to represent the individual and match with skeletal data. Weights aligning with recorded pregnancy or lactation were not used, instead the maximum weight before or after these events was used. Likewise, female weights showing a clear spike during subadult or adulthood (possible pregnancy) were not used to represent the individual.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Descriptive statistics and analytical statistics were conducted using R (R Core Team, 2022) and figures using ggplot package (Wickham, 2016). Number of individuals, means and standard deviations of measurements are reported. Pearson’s correlation and resulting p-values were used to assess whether the Cayo Santiago macaques exhibited significant temporal trends in long bone and diaphyseal measures (α = 0.05). Specifically, Pearson’s correlation was used to examine the associations between individuals’ skeletal measurements (long bone lengths, diaphyseal dimensions and body weights) and their date of births. Bonferroni corrections were employed to ensure that the results of the 25 Pearson’s correlations were not overly interpreted, resulting in a threshold of significance of α = 0.002. Date of birth is employed as a continuous variable to frame the temporal effects of the Cayo Santiago climate in the population over time. The study’s design, due to the lack of a north Indian-origin control sample, and the time period of which this study covers (51 years), is geared toward testing transgenerational effects of acclimation on skeletal sizes in the population (Donelan et al, 2020). Underlying our hypothesis, we assume the effects of acclimation will exhibit a secular trend due to a tendency toward necessary thermoregulatory equilibrium and the inability of the organism to observably achieve this within or over a single generation. Transgenerational plasticity is implicit in many notable studies that investigate secular trends of growth and development within human populations (Cole, 2000; Emanuel et al, 2004; Matrorell and Zongrone, 2012), the mechanism of which is not directly tested here.

Given the relatively limited sample size of body weights (n = 105) available to us, which includes skeletally immature individuals that are unsuited and not used in this study, a suitable skeletal proxy was sought that could represent body weight for the entire sample (n = 635). Pearson’s correlation of several cranial and postcranial measurements, as well as the geometric mean (GM) - a combined value of multiple cranial and postcranial measurements (1–24 in Table 2), was conducted to find a suitable skeletal proxy in this subsample (n = 105) that would allow us to explore trends in body weight in the entire sample over time. Known body weights were then regressed onto the chosen skeletal proxy using several candidate models, including linear, quadratic, log-linear, and log-log transformations. Measurement values of the chosen skeletal proxy were fitted onto the best-fit regression model to produce body weight values for the entire sample. These were then used to examine body weight trends over time to ultimately test for acclimation.

Multiple regressions (α = 0.05) were used to further assess the impact of age on skeletal size and to parse its potential relationship with Date of Birth. Although, all individuals are classified as adults in this sample based on complete long bone epiphyseal fusion, it is apparent that those with the most recent date of births are represented by younger adult individuals compared to the earliest born individuals due to the fact that the oldest adult individuals of those born to more recently are still living on the island and are not yet accessioned in the skeletal collection. Therefore, it is possible the age skew within the, purely adult, sample may influence temporal skeletal measurement trends that may otherwise relate to Date of Birth and possible acclimation. With skeletal size as the dependent variable, Age at Death, Date of Birth, and the interaction between Age at Death and Date of Birth as the independent variables, multiple regressions were conducted for each skeletal measure and body weight proxy for males and females separately.

sec.title: Absolute Trends
sec.p: The log-log transformation of body weight and bizygomatic breadth produced the highest R² values for both males (R² = 0.88) and females (R² = 0.91) (Table 4), and were subsequently used to explore body weight trends for the entire sample. Although exhibiting a lower predictive power of body weight than single-skeletal measurements, including bizygomatic breadth, the relationship between weight and GM was still strong (Table 4) and itself holds inherent advantages over single measurement proxies (Lewton, 2015; Gordon et al, 2008). In light of this, a parallel set of results using GM as a skeletal proxy for body weight, instead of bizygomatic breadth, are reported in Appendix.
Overall trends in long bone length, diaphyseal circumference and body weight significantly declined in the Cayo Santiago populations over the 1951–2002 date of birth time period investigated here.

Long bone measurements all decrease over time in males (r = -0.18 to -0.26) (Table 4; Fig. 2). Whereas corresponding female measurements show very little fluctuation according to their date of birth (r = 0.00 to 0.07). Measures of long bones circumferences all decreased in both males (r = -0.16 to -0.33) and females (r = -0.19 to -0.37) over time (Table 4; Fig. 3). In contrast to long bone lengths, diaphyseal circumference trends run close to parallel between sexes over time. Body weight decreased over time (Table 4; Fig. 4), with females’ declining by 2.22kg (r = -0.33) and males by 0.98kg (r = -0.14).

Multiple regression analysis (Table 5) indicated that Date of Birth was a significant driver of skeletal size and trends depicted in Figs. 2–4. Date of birth exhibited a significant and negative relationship with all male long bone length and diaphyseal circumference values (except radial circumference). Age at Death was significantly and positively associated with male body weight, but not Date of Birth as Fig. 4 suggests. For females, multiple regression analysis supported all trends visualized in Figs. 2–4. Date of Birth exhibited no relationship with female long bone lengths (excluding radial lengths) and a significant and negative relationship with diaphyseal circumferences and body weights. Age at Death also exhibited a positive relationship with radial circumference and body weight, as did the interaction of Age at Death and Date of Birth for all female circumference values.

sec.title: Ratio Trends
sec.p: Males exhibit minor and positive trends of long bone length/body weight over time (Fig. 5). Females, in contrast, exhibit strong and positive trends for the same ratios (r = 0.34 to 0.36). Long bone diaphyseal dimension trends exhibit a similar pattern relative to body weight. Male trends are static over time, while females exhibit moderate and positive increases of diaphyseal dimensions relative to body weight over time (r = 0.18 to 0.28) (Fig. 6). Similarly, female long bone lengths relative to diaphyseal dimensions exhibit moderate to strong positive trends (r = 0.17 to 0.38) (Fig. 7). Males range from static to moderate positive trends for the same ratio (r = 0.0062 to 0.04).

The brachial and crural indices show minor negative and positive trends, respectively, in both males and females (Fig 8a and b). Accordingly, proximal/distal limb segment ratios have not varied much over the 50+ years of the colony. Contrastingly, male intermembral indices ratios exhibit a significant and positive trend over time, whereas females remain relatively constant. As with absolute long bone lengths, male intermembral indices are converging on female ratios over time (Fig 8c).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Overall temporal trends in the bodily dimensions of the Cayo Santiago rhesus macaque population suggests that they have acclimated to their more tropical island conditions since arriving from northern India in 1938. This was evidenced by significantly decreasing female body weights, with the same pattern exhibited in males, and in turn an increasing surface area to volume ratio and rate at which they expel heat from the body. Females have further increased heat dissipation via limb dimensions. Female long bone lengths have remained static while body weight and diaphyseal circumferences have greatly declined over the same period. Long bone lengths have also increased relative to diaphyseal circumferences. Taken together, female limbs have gradually become leaner, increasing in length relative to circumference and body weight. Therefore, female trends conform to both Bergmann’s and Allen’s rules. Male trends conform less convincingly to both, but particularly this latter principle, as diaphyseal circumference, long bone length and body weights decline at near parallel rates over time. Overall, there is strong evidence that Cayo Santiago population has acclimatized to their homogenously warm, sunlight-rich, and sea-level island conditions over the past 50 years by increasing the rate at which they expel heat via a gradual reduction in body size and altering body proportions.

Our results align with expectations of a population acclimating to warmer, more equatorial conditions (Bergmann, 1847; Allen, 1877). This study supports previous works on translocated primate populations (Paterson, 1996; Clarke and O’Neil, 1999) as well as the effect of broader thermoregulatory principles on primate morphological variation within species (Fooden and Albrecht, 1993; Buck et al, 2018; Huffman et al, 2020) and between species (Fooden, 1997; Fooden and Albrecht, 1999; Ravosa, 2007; Weinstein, 2011; Turner et al, 2018). Although contradictory in conclusion, and indeed findings for long bone to body weight ratio, our results exhibit some alignment with Weinstein’s (2011) regarding intralimb indices and their near inertia between samples or over time. In another comparable study, Antón et al (2016) employed a control sample consisting of a limited number of wild-shot Indian Rhesus macaques yet found Cayo Santiago individuals to be larger somatically and skeletally similar in size. Indeed, the disparity between their origin conditions and those of Cayo Santiago would not intuitively elicit the trends observed in this study. Despite being farther from the equator, at a higher altitude and receiving less sunlight, the annual average temperature of the city of Lucknow is 2°C warmer than that of Cayo Santiago. Assuming the trends observed in this study are driven by acclimatory processes, explanations turn to the more divergent patterns of seasonality between the two locations as a likely cause.

The relationship between heightened seasonality (annual temperature range), larger body sizes and metabolically mediated fasting capabilities (Turner et al, 2018; Henzi et al, 2017), serves as a plausible explanation for body weight trends observed here. Larger individuals, due to a lower metabolism in colder surroundings, accumulate fat and metabolize it more slowly, exhibiting greater energy efficiency than their smaller counterparts thus allowing for greater fasting and survival capabilities in seasonal environments (Nigenda-Morales et al, 2018). In terms of a direct effect, it is also possible that the absence of Lucknow’s coldest temperatures diminished the necessity for core temperature regulation and resulted in the declining body weights observed in the Cayo Santiago population (Aschoff, 1981; Lubbe et al, 2014; Henzi et al, 2017; Turner et al, 2018).

The minimum, or coldest, temperatures an organism’s habitat has been singled out as a climatic metric effective at eliciting a targeted morphological response or adaptation. This is evident in the wealth of studies that show climatic signals are solely correlated with cold-adapted human populations (Roseman and Weaver, 2004; Harvarti and Weaver, 2006; Foster and Collard, 2013; Buck et al, 2018). The lowest average temperature of the coldest month between Lucknow (8°C) and Cayo Santiago (19°C), differ substantially, with the Indian region, through the aid of northerly wind chills, infrequently experiencing freezing temperatures (Bonavia, 1885; Singh et al, 2012). Therefore, it may that the coldest experienced temperatures have a stronger influence on morphological acclimation via both Bergmann’s and Allen’s rules (Weinstein, 2011; Martinez et al, 2013; Collier et al, 2019; Fan et al, 2019). After their translocation to Cayo Santiago, it is possible the ambient temperatures of the populations new surroundings alleviated this pressure imposed by the coldest extremes of their original habitat and their body weight and proportions adjusted accordingly.

A greater crural index is associated with acclimation to warmer environments, decreasing body sizes and terrestrial cursoriality. Therefore, increasing crural index scores observed in females may represent acclimation to Cayo Santiago or maintenance of allometric proportions with body weight (Jungers, 1985; Strasser, 1992). All other intralimb indicines for males and females exhibit a stasis (female brachial and male crural indices) or decline (male brachial index) over time, suggesting there is no one driver of intralimb trends in the Cayo Santiago population. The intermembral index trends of the population run counter to previous findings that the forelimb should increase, relative to the hindlimb, with increasing body size (Biegert and Maurer, 1972; Aiello, 1981; Rollinson and Martin, 1981; Dykyj, 1982; Jungers, 1985). Male trends increase under conditions of decreasing body sizes, while female intermembral index remains static under more pronounced declines in body weight, resulting in a convergence on approximately 0.86 (forelimb/hindlimb length multiplied by 100) over time (Fig. 8c).

The strength of the observed temporal trends differs between sexes in the Cayo Santiago population. To our knowledge, pronounced female acclimation has not been explicitly addressed in the literature. There have been indications in the morphometry of both translocated populations and those examining the wider ecogeographic principles (Clarke and O’Neil, 1999; Weinstein, 2011; Volynchik, 2014; Turner et al, 2018), although the same studies find a mix of male and female measurements congruent with acclimation. Sex differences in morphology or process are often accounted for by sex-specific socio-behavioral factors (Clarke and O’Neil, 1999; Ito et al, 2014). The rich context and inherent accessibility surrounding the Cayo Santiago population allows for robust inferences on the potential influences of socio-behavioral processes on the observed sex differences in body weight and proportions over time.

In contrast to many other species (Clutton-Brock et al, 1978; Breuer et al, 2012), male body size does not equate to reproductive success in rhesus macaques, as male dominance is predominantly achieved by queuing rather than fighting (Dubuc, 2011; Kimock et al, 2019). There are in fact multiple pathways to reproductive success in the Cayo Santiago Rhesus macaques, including consortships and sneaky mating (Berard et al, 1994; Higham and Maestripieri, 2014; Kimock et al 2019). Resultantly, the effects of male-male competition on body size in rhesus macaques is less than in species that rely more directly on male conflict for mate access (Higham and Maestripieri, 2014). Efforts to recapitulate wild male:female sex ratios (Hernández-Pacheco et al, 2013) at Cayo Santiago may have further reduced male-male competition in the population. The disproportionate removal of males since 1984 has seen the male percentage of the adults in the population fall from close to 57%, under a slight male birth skew (Rawlins and Kessler, 1986b; Rawlins and Kessler, 1986c; Hoffman et a, 2008), to below 40% in recent years (Hoffman et al, 2008). Therefore, the reduced proportion of adult males may have contributed to the slight decline in body weights via reduced male competition levels (Hoffman et al, 2008; Hernández-Pacheco et al, 2016), though competition may have still served to buffer against the more dramatic and significant temporal declines observed in females. Feeding competition may also be partly responsible for the disparate trends in body weight sex. Not all individuals or groups enjoy equal access to resources in the Cayo Santiago population, despite being provisioned (Maestripieri and Georgiev, 2016). High levels of within-group and between-group female conflict has been reported according to group size, while dominant females have been known to control resources in the largest groups (Balasubramaniam et al, 2014). Increasing population density in the island population may be favoring a resource monopoly in a small and dominant number of individuals while the rest of the colony is left with less, under increased acts of female-female aggression (Maestripieri and Georgiev, 2016). The same population trends may have also had an indirect effect on body weight. Members of different social groups tend to avoid one another’s territory (Carpenter and Krakower, 1941; Boelkins and Wilson, 1972). Coupled with the expanding population and number of social groups (Kanthaswamy et al, 2017), individuals have increasingly less area to roam over the 15.2-acre island. Therefore, reduced activity levels may have contributed to body weight declines observed in this study.

Even more stark sex disparities exist in the trends of long bones. All measured long bone lengths in males decline at similar rates (r = -0.26 to -0.18) as do females’ exhibit stagnation at similar rates (r = -0.053 to 0.0039). This indicates females exhibit a stronger relationship with Allen’s rule than in males. Outside of thermoregulatory explanations, there is no obvious functional alternative as to why male long bone lengths differ so significantly from females, other than their allometric constraints to the buffering effects of body weights already posited. Independent of mechanism, however, there are functional consequences. Longer relative limb lengths have been associated with a reduced cost of transport in quadrupedal mammals. Among cercopithecines, longer relative limbs generate greater walking speeds at lower stride and angular excursion levels (Polk, 2004), as well as more extended postures that facilitate mechanical advantages of the extensor muscles (Biewener, 1989; Polk, 2002). Increasing relative diaphyseal dimensions in females (r = 0.19 to 0.28) also pose differing trends to that of males (r = 0.083 to 0.027). This runs counter to the proposed direction of acclimation, including Weinstein’s (2011) findings that warmer-residing macaque species exhibit greater relative joint diameters than those in colder climates. Given the twofold decrease in female to male macaque body weight, it seems likely that female diaphyseal dimensions exhibited a relative increase either as an allometric constraint (Egi, 2001; Campione and Evans, 2012; Nadell et al, 2021) to facilitate stability or movement, rather than indications of physical activity (Ruff and Runestad, 1992; Lieberman et al, 2001), or locomotion preference (Godfrey et al, 1991).

A limitation of the current study is the absence of a control sample from the region of the original population in Lucknow, India. It is assumed that the earliest members in this sample are closer representatives of the origin population than those in later years. Whereas trends uncovered here may be in response to anthropogenically-induced climate change the colony has experienced over the past 80 years. Although, the nearest municipality, Humacao, has seen less than 1°C rise in temperature over the study period. (source: https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/country/puerto-rico/trends-variability-historical). On the other side of this, the data cited in this study for Lucknow, India, pertains to recent climatic data and it is apparent that temperatures are far warmer now than they were when the colony was shipped in 1938 (Basha et al, 2017; Sanjay et al, 2020). Therefore, the climatic data underpinning our hypothesis are conservative figures to the reality experienced over 80 years ago. Extraneous colony factors may have also confounded our interpretation, including population bottlenecks (McMillan and Duggleby, 1981; Kanthaswamy et al, 2017), nutrition (Wang, 2012), hurricanes (Morcillo et al, 2020), and removal strategies (Hernández-Pacheco et al, 2016). Further exploration of these factors is warranted to uncover the processes that have shaped colony health and morphology over its long history. Doing so is especially important for males, as they appear to be less influenced by the process of acclimation. Future studies may also wish to take advantage of the matrilineal data associated with many of the individuals in the Cayo Santiago skeletal collection. Secular changes in body proportions may be further elucidated by comparisons within and between matrilines in order to illuminate generational differences in a familial context, and to test for the effect of matrilineal dominance rank.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: The Cayo Santiago macaque population have shown evidence of acclimation to the equatorial, tropical, island since transportation from their north Indian origins in 1938, supporting our hypothesis. Results demonstrated that male and female macaques have decreased in body weight by 0.98kg and 2.22kg, respectively, over the time period from 1951 to 2002. Females exhibit stronger and further evidence of acclimation through bodily proportions, by increasing limb length relative to body weight and diaphyseal circumferences. These align with Bergmann’s and Allen’s rule, in the direction of acclimating to a warmer environment by increasing surface area to volume and increasing heat expenditure. Male long bone lengths, diaphyses and body weights tracked almost parallel over time, indicating some mechanism of constraint on changing bodily proportions. Therefore, the majority of our predictions were also borne out, particularly in females. Uncovering acclimation in the Cayo Santiago macaques not only holds consequence for the future of this important population, but to the morphological trajectories of humans, non-human-primates, and all lifeforms facing rapidly changing climates.

sec.title: ABSOLUTE TRENDS
sec.p: Using the equation derived from the log-log regression detailed in Table 3, known GM values were input to generate body weight trends in the entire sample. Body weight decreased over time (Figure A1), with females’ declining by 1.38kg (r = −0.20; p = 0.0001) and males by 1.12 kg (r = −0.12; p = 0.1). Multiple regression analysis of body weight exhibited a significant and negative relationship with Date of Birth in alignment with the trends in Figure A1. Incongruent with correlational analysis in Figure A1, body weight was also significantly and negatively associated with male date of birth in the multiple regression. This suggests that age at death and the interaction of date of birth and age at death (both being significant) may have an influence on male long bone lengths in the sample.

sec.label: A.2 |
sec.title: RATIO TRENDS
sec.p: Males exhibit minor and positive trends of long bone length/body weight over time (Figure A2) using GM as a skeletal proxy for body weight, in a similar fashion to those of the main text where bizygomatic breadth was instead employed. Female long bone length/body weight over time likewise mirror those of the main text, though tend exhibit less of a decline over the same period. For diaphyseal dimensions (Figure A3), the same pattern is borne out of those in long bone length ratios and those of the main text for the same variables: significant declines over the time period of study for females, and stasis for males. The only exception is that humerus circumference/body weight exhibits a similar stasis to their male counterparts using GM as a body weight proxy.

caption.p: Length and diaphyseal circumference measurements taken of four long bones. Length measurements represent the absolute maximum distance from the most inferior to the most superior aspects of the long bones. Diaphyseal measurements consisted of finding the midpoint of the long bone by first measuring absolute length and dividing that number in half. The diaphyses measurements are defined as the halfway point of the maximum length of the bone for the humerus (HD), radius (RD), femur (FD) and tibia (TD). These measurements were taken using a tape measure to the nearest millimeter. Humerus length (HL) consisted of placing the outer jaws of the callipers mediolaterally on the trochlea and capitulum and the inner callipers on the most superior aspect of the humeral head. Radius length (RL) consisted of placing the outer jaws of the callipers on the most inferior aspect of the radial styloid and the inner callipers on the depression within the radial head. Femur length (FL) consisted of placing the outer jaws of the caliper mediolaterally across the condyles with inner jaws resting on the superior tip of the greater trochanter. Infrequently, the femoral head would represent the most superior aspect of the bone. Tibia length (TL) consisted of placing the outer jaws of the callipers on the most inferior aspect of the medial malleolus and the inner callipers on the most superior aspect of the intercondylar eminence. Layout of image inspired by Onar and Belli (2005).
